summary: Japanese virgin's bower, also called sweet autumn clematis, is a garden vine that can climb 30 feet when it has support. It grows so fast and so heavily that in natural areas it can smother mature trees and push out native plants. It is on New York's regulated list, which means it may still be sold and planted, but not where it threatens natural areas, and it must be sold with signs saying it is invasive. It looks very much like the native virgin's bower, but you can tell them apart because the native species has toothed and lobed leaves instead of smooth-edged ones.
history: Autumn clematis is native to Japan and China and was brought to North America to be grown as an ornamental plant. People continue to plant it in gardens today because of its many small white flowers and feathery seedheads.
seasons: In spring, new shoots emerge from the woody stems that grew the year before. The plant produces abundant small white flowers with four petals in August, making it easy to identify at that time. By late September, the flowers develop into silvery, feathery seedheads that curl and spread through the wind.

handling.text: Plants and their roots can be dug out, but root pieces may resprout and seeds in the soil can keep sprouting for some time, so repeat visits may be needed. Planting the native virgin's bower instead gives a similar look without the invasive risk. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
